The views and opinions of authors expressed herein do not necessarily state or reflect those of the United States Government or any agency thereof. 2 Executive Summary This project was funded by the Bioenergy Engineering for Product Synthesis (BEEPS) program under the Funding Opportunity Announcement (FOA) DE-FOA-0001916 Topic Area 5 “Rewiring Carbon Utilization”. This FOA sought projects that would electrocatalytically reduce CO to a carbon intermediate and then upconvert to a multi- 2 carbon product or fuel via non-photosynthetic biological system engineering. The project sought to combine the expertise of OCO Chem, whose chief scientist had previously developed an efficient electrocatalytic reactor for conversion of CO to formate with 2 potential to scale, Montana State University investigators who had recently patented a method for laterally grading membranes with the potential of improving reactant distribution and more uniform efficiency across membrane-based reactors, and University of South Florida which had recently discovered a novel C-C bond forming reaction not known to naturally occur in biological systems and which uses C1 substrates and circumvents the central microbial metabolism. Electrochemical Conversion Scaling of catalytic membranes where membrane efficiency does not substantially drop with size is problematic, where dual phase flows and species concentration can change. For CO -formate membranes, this is realized as a change in concentration of gas 2 phase, integration of gas delivery membrane and catalytic membrane, edge effects in fuel delivery, mechanical support of the catalytic membrane, and tortuosity of the porous membrane that drives device performance. Further, membrane technology is constrained by the integration of multiple materials and interfaces, where an opportunity lies in developing multi-functional membranes that provide the entire suite of functionality within a single layer of material. Mass transfer limitations for gaseous reactants liquid-solid multiphase media arise due to restrictions in traditional porous media, are evident in numerous electrochemical technologies, and are a fundamental barrier to the scalable efficiency of layered device architecture. While methodologies exist to manipulate porosity and pore morphology in electrochemical support structures and integrated active materials, a key challenge is addressing both axial and lateral pore gradients in fluid diffusion layers. No materials processing technology existed at the start of this project that was capable of generating continuous lateral pore gradients (along the length of a porous membrane with respect to fluid influx) within gas diffusion layers to provide uniform product delivery and byproduct removal over large-scale catalyst systems. Montana State University (MSU) modified its freeze tape casting process to produce porous layers with low tortuosity pores and laterally graded total pore volume to optimize mass transfer. Freeze tape casting (FTC), which is a combination of ice templating and traditional tape casting, is a scalable, materials-agnostic approach for processing large area, thin membranes with a graded and low tortuosity path through the cross-section.
